- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next 5–7 days.
- If model shows sharp upward spike followed by forecasted decline, actual price often reverses earlier — adjust downward 1–3% in 3–5 day horizon.
- If sentiment turns negative (≤0.33) after a peak, model often fails to correct quickly — apply mean reversion bias: subtract 1–3% from forecast for next 7–10 days.
- Model underestimates prices when sentiment is neutral or negative and recent history shows downward trend — add 0.5–1.5% to forecast for next 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is within 1–2% of true outcome for last 3–5 days, assume model is “calibrated” — no adjustment needed unless sentiment shifts sharply.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome shows strong downward trend after a peak, model often overcorrects — reduce forecast by 2–4% for next 10–15 days.
- If sentiment history shows multiple 1.00 entries (strong bullish), model often overestimates — apply 1–3% downward correction for next 7–10 days.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome for 3–5 consecutive days, apply “mean reversion” rule: subtract 0.5–1.5% per day until price stabilizes.
- If sentiment is negative and model forecast is flat or slightly rising, model often misses downward momentum — reduce forecast by 1–2% for next 5–7 days.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if true outcome shows volatility > 3% from mean, model often fails to capture it — adjust forecast to align with recent 7-day moving average.
